title: Handheld Canon Focus Stacking, Sun-Star Beams, and Advanced Color Grading (NZ4-3)
summary: This video guides a photographer through a complete post-production workflow on a high-dynamic-range landscape shot assembled from multiple RAW frames captured handheld with a Canon system. Techniques demonstrated include: preparing RAW files for focus stacking by expanding dynamic range and adjusting exposure, assembling and aligning a handheld focus stack, and blending layers for a sharp composite. The presenter then selects, clones, and refines sun-beam artifacts, uses mid-tone dodging and selective color adjustments to enhance foreground and sky tonality, applies an Auto HDR-style treatment, and finishes with color grading, a controlled vignette, and careful compositional refinements. The segment also dives into advanced warp-based tools (convex/concave, trapezoid, puppet warp) to exaggerate mountain shapes and perspective while warning about horizon straightness, before discussing fog insertion and final crop decisions. Throughout, the emphasis is on deliberate, incremental adjustments and maintaining balance between foreground, beams, and sky to preserve naturalism while maximizing depth and visual impact.

sections.title: RAW prep and dynamic-range expansion for focus stacking
concepts: Camera Raw expansion of dynamic range
sections.description: The speaker begins by opening multiple files in Camera Raw, expanding the dynamic range and lowering exposure before stacking. This preps the frames for later alignment and blend, with emphasis on maintaining the intended tonal balance before the stack is created.

sections.title: Handheld focus stacking workflow and alignment
sections.description: Images are loaded into a stack and aligned automatically. The presenter highlights improved speed and accuracy when using Canon’s 10 frames-per-second performance for handheld focus stacks, and then demonstrates loading and auto-aligning the frames before the automatic blend step.

sections.title: Initial post-stack review and composition framing
sections.description: Post-stack steps include deselecting, flattening the stack, and cropping to a four-by-five framing. The narrator comments on composition, highlighting edge framing and the balance of elements such as trees and openings as crucial before further refinements.

sections.title: Sun star beams and cloud matching via cloning
sections.description: A sun-star beam is re-created by selecting a shot with an existing sun star, applying a previous conversion, and cloning the beam into the target area. The clouds are matched to maintain seamless continuity, using soft brushes and careful masking to preserve low-detail areas.

sections.title: Mid-tone light adjustments and auto HDR refinements
sections.description: The workflow tightens the mid-ground light by darkening areas then painting in whites to brighten shadows while avoiding highlights. Auto HDR-style steps are applied to beams and mid-ground to boost clarity, followed by cloning and blending to emphasize beam structure without affecting highlight integrity.

sections.title: Color refinement, saturation control, and selective color
sections.description: A sequence of local color edits emphasizes foliage and sunset tones. The sponge tool adds side-light to leaves, while HSL and selective-color work nudge saturation and luminance in specific regions. The presenter demonstrates preserving the fjord’s color while altering the trees and sky to guide the viewer’s eye.

sections.title: Color grading and sky-tint balance
sections.description: A warm highlight color is added with targeted balance to confine adjustments to highlights, followed by cool shadows and subtle mid-tone tweaks. The color grading process is explained in terms of luminosity, amount, and blending, trading off color in the sky against the mountains to preserve separation and depth.

sections.title: Final vignette and flow adjustments
sections.description: A three-step dark blur vignette is applied, and the original image is painted back into the vignette to preserve natural light flow and direct the viewer’s eye toward the beam-rich middle ground, heightening the three-dimensional feel.

sections.title: Warp tools deep-dive: trapezoids, perspective, and puppet warp
sections.description: A detailed exploration of warp tools demonstrates how to magnify mountains using convex/concave warps and the rule of trapezoids to simulate lens distortion. The presenter reviews perspective warp, its impact on image sharpness, and puppet warp, including anchoring points to avoid unwanted distortion. Cautions include preserving straight horizons and natural geometry, with thoughts on when puppet warp is appropriate (non-permanent subjects) versus when to avoid over-warping landscape geology.

sections.title: Final considerations: lens behavior, cropping, and fog integration
sections.description: The session concludes with reminders about lens-induced distortion, the utility of placing the horizon thoughtfully, and a discussion of fog as a method to separate layers and unify composition. The presenter notes the balance between foreground and sky color, suggests cropped adjustments to improve symmetry, and points toward fog as a prime candidate for future shots.
